The Dependent Chip Model (DCM) redefines tournament equity by treating player survival as a conditional probability dependent on current chip stacks, unlike the Independent Chip Model (ICM) which assumes independent survival. This recursive formulation captures the non-linear impact of stack depth on strategic play, particularly in late-stage tournaments where large blinds amplify the risk of elimination. Mathematically, it transforms the static ICM valuation into a dynamic survival-weighted expectation, yielding higher equity assignments for top finish positions and lower equity for lower placements. The key failure mode arises when the equal-skill assumption breaks down, leading to biased equity estimates that can distort optimal deal-making strategies.

This asymmetry creates exploitable biases in chop negotiations, especially when one player holds a dominant chip lead.
